The '''vector triple product''' is the [[cross product]] of one vector with the cross product of two others, $\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$. Its value is a linear combination of $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$, so it lies in the plane these two vectors span.

It differs from the [[Cross product#Scalar triple product|scalar triple product]] $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$, which is a scalar.

== Formal definition ==

For $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$,

{{#content:Q2274}}

where $\times$ denotes the [[cross product]] and $\cdot$ the [[dot product]].<ref>{{#cite:Q2329}}</ref>

<blockquote>
Equivalently,

$$
\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\,\vec{b}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\,\vec{c},
$$

often memorised as the '''BAC-CAB rule''': the two terms list the same three vectors in the orders $\vec{b},\vec{a},\vec{c}$ and $\vec{c},\vec{a},\vec{b}$. The symbol $\wedge$ denotes the same cross product as $\times$.
</blockquote>

{{Hidden proof}}
Write $\vec{a}=(a_1,a_2,a_3)$, $\vec{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3)$, and $\vec{c}=(c_1,c_2,c_3)$. By the [[Cross product#Formal definition|definition of the cross product]],

$$
\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=(b_2c_3-b_3c_2,\; b_3c_1-b_1c_3,\; b_1c_2-b_2c_1).
$$

The first component of $\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bigl(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\bigr)_{1}
&=a_2(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)-a_3(b_3c_1-b_1c_3)\\
&=a_2b_1c_2+a_3b_1c_3-(a_2b_2+a_3b_3)c_1,
\end{aligned}
$$

while the first component of the right-hand side $(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bigl((\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}\bigr)_{1}
&=(a_1c_1+a_2c_2+a_3c_3)b_1-(a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3)c_1\\
&=a_1b_1c_1+a_2b_1c_2+a_3b_1c_3-a_1b_1c_1-(a_2b_2+a_3b_3)c_1\\
&=a_2b_1c_2+a_3b_1c_3-(a_2b_2+a_3b_3)c_1,
\end{aligned}
$$

the terms $a_1b_1c_1$ having cancelled. The first components agree. Relabelling the indices cyclically, $(1,2,3)\to(2,3,1)\to(3,1,2)$, carries the first-component computation onto the second and third components without changing the form of either side, so the two sides are equal in all three components.
{{End hidden}}

== Reversed nesting ==

The bracket cannot be moved freely: for $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$,

$$
(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\vec{c}=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\,\vec{b}-(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})\,\vec{a}.
$$

{{Hidden proof}}
By anti-commutativity of the cross product (see [[Cross product#Properties|properties of the cross product]]),

$$
(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\vec{c}=-\vec{c}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}).
$$

Applying the identity with $(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c})$ replaced by $(\vec{c},\vec{a},\vec{b})$,

$$
\vec{c}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})=(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{b})\,\vec{a}-(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a})\,\vec{b},
$$

hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\vec{c}
&=-(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{b})\,\vec{a}+(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a})\,\vec{b}\\
&=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\,\vec{b}-(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})\,\vec{a},
\end{aligned}
$$

by commutativity of the dot product.
{{End hidden}}

<blockquote>
The two nestings differ in general. For $\vec{a}=\vec{b}=\vec{i}$ and $\vec{c}=\vec{j}$,

$$
\vec{i}\times(\vec{i}\times\vec{j})=-\vec{j},
\qquad
(\vec{i}\times\vec{i})\times\vec{j}=\vec{0}.
$$
</blockquote>

== Geometric interpretation ==

$$
\begin{cases}
\bigl(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\bigr)\cdot\vec{a}=0\\[4pt]
\bigl(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\bigr)\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=0
\end{cases}
$$

Since $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ is normal to the plane spanned by $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ (see [[Cross product#Orthogonality|orthogonality of the cross product]]), the vector triple product lies in that plane; the identity shows this directly through its right-hand side, a combination of $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$. Being also orthogonal to $\vec{a}$, it is the vector of that plane orthogonal to $\vec{a}$, and it vanishes when the two conditions cannot both be met:

$$
\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=\vec{0}\iff\vec{a}\parallel\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\ \text{or}\ \vec{b}\parallel\vec{c}.
$$

== Example ==

{{Hidden example}}
For $\vec{a}=(1,2,4)$, $\vec{b}=(2,2,0)$, and $\vec{c}=(1,3,0)$,

$$
\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=2+4+0=6,
\qquad
\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=1+6+0=7,
$$

so the identity gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})
&=7\,(2,2,0)-6\,(1,3,0)\\
&=(14,14,0)-(6,18,0)\\
&=(8,-4,0).
\end{aligned}
$$

Directly from the definition,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{b}\times\vec{c}&=(2\cdot 0-0\cdot 3,\; 0\cdot 1-2\cdot 0,\; 2\cdot 3-2\cdot 1)=(0,0,4),\\
\vec{a}\times(0,0,4)&=(2\cdot 4-4\cdot 0,\; 4\cdot 0-1\cdot 4,\; 1\cdot 0-2\cdot 0)=(8,-4,0).
\end{aligned}
$$
{{End hidden}}

== Applications ==

'''Acceleration in rotation.''' A point of a rigid body rotating with angular velocity $\vec{\omega}$ about a fixed point $O$ has velocity $\vec{v}=\vec{\omega}\times\vec{r}$, so the centripetal part of its acceleration is

$$
\vec{\omega}\times(\vec{\omega}\times\vec{r})=(\vec{\omega}\cdot\vec{r})\,\vec{\omega}-|\vec{\omega}|^{2}\,\vec{r}.
$$

Writing $\hat{\vec{\omega}}=\vec{\omega}/|\vec{\omega}|$ and $\vec{r}_{\perp}=\vec{r}-(\vec{r}\cdot\hat{\vec{\omega}})\hat{\vec{\omega}}$ for the part of $\vec{r}$ perpendicular to the axis, the right-hand side collapses to

$$
\vec{\omega}\times(\vec{\omega}\times\vec{r})=-|\vec{\omega}|^{2}\,\vec{r}_{\perp},
$$

the axial part $(\vec{r}\cdot\hat{\vec{\omega}})\hat{\vec{\omega}}$ cancelling.

'''Angular momentum of a rotating body.''' The integrand $\vec{r}\times(\vec{\omega}\times\vec{r})$ is expanded with the same identity in the derivation of the [[Inertia matrix]].
